about.p: This course goes with *English Pronunciation in Use Intermediate*. It follows the book's sixty units in three parts: the sounds of English and how they are spelt; syllables, word stress and sentence stress; and the pronunciation of real conversation – grouping, emphasis and tones.

Every word and example has a sound button, and the listening questions use your device's British voice. The phonemic symbols, such as /æ/ or /ð/, show exactly which sound to make – Reference 1 lists them all.

At intermediate level, pronunciation is as much about listening as speaking. Fast, natural English joins words, drops sounds and squeezes small words – the units on joining words, weak forms and tones will help you understand native speakers as well as sound clearer yourself.
You don't need to do the units in order. Reference 2 is a short self-test to help you find the units you need most, and Reference 3 lists the points that matter most for Korean speakers.

about.tip: Record yourself whenever you can. Compare your recording with the sound button, one detail at a time – a vowel, a stress, a tune.

L.p: English spelling is an old record of how words used to sound, so it is a poor guide to how they sound today. The same letters can stand for different sounds – *ough* in *though*, *through*, *tough* and *cough* – and the same sound can be spelt in several ways: *buy*, *bye* and *by* all sound the same.
There are still useful patterns, though, and the most useful is the one in this unit: whether a vowel letter says its own name, or makes its short sound.

L.h: A the vowel says its name, as in "late"

L.p: When a single vowel letter is followed by one consonant and a silent *e*, it usually says its alphabet name: *a* /eɪ/, *e* /iː/, *i* /aɪ/, *o* /əʊ/, *u* /juː/.

L.say: Pete hopes to take the late tube home at nine.

L.h: B the short sound, as in "mat"

L.p: Without the silent *e* – especially when the word ends in a consonant, or the consonant is doubled (*hopping*) – the vowel is usually short: /æ/, /e/, /ɪ/, /ɒ/, /ʌ/.

L.say: Tim's pet cat hid in the hot tub.

L.p: Homophones are spelt differently but sound the same: *right* and *write*, *hour* and *our*, *piece* and *peace*. In speech, the situation tells you which word is meant.

L.tip: Korean speakers: the habit of reading English letter by letter, as you would read Hangul, causes many errors. When you meet a new word, check its symbols or its sound before you say it aloud for the first time – the first way you say a word is the way you will remember it.

L.x: *come* breaks the pattern: it is */kʌm/* (not */kəʊm/*).
*give* breaks the pattern too: it is */gɪv/* (not */gaɪv/*).

L.p: /eɪ/ and /æ/ are both spelt with the letter *a*, so spelling alone will not tell you which one to use. /eɪ/ is a diphthong that glides; /æ/ is a short, open vowel that stays still.

Start with /e/ and glide up towards /ɪ/, as one syllable. Common spellings: *a* + consonant + *e* (*plane*), *ai* (*main*), *ay* (*day*), *ei* (*weight*), *ey* (*they*), and *ea* in *great*, *break* and *steak*.

L.say: The neighbour's favourite station is on the main train line.

L.p: Drop your jaw low, spread your lips and keep the sound still. It is spelt *a*, often before a double consonant (*latter*, *carry*) or a final consonant (*plan*).

L.say: Have you planned a Spanish salad for the family?

L.p: Compare *main* and *man*, *later* and *latter*, *snake* and *snack*. If you hear a glide, it is /eɪ/; if the vowel is short and still, it is /æ/.

L.say: I'll have a snack later, but not a snake!

L.tip: Korean speakers: 메인 is two syllables, but *main* is one, with a glide. And /æ/ needs a much wider mouth than 애 – open it as wide as for 아, with your lips spread.

L.x: *have* breaks the spelling pattern: it is */hæv/* (not */heɪv/*).

L.p: /b/ and /p/ are made in the same place – both lips – but in English the difference between them is not mainly the voice. It is a puff of air.
Close your lips and release them gently, with no puff of air. Between vowels, as in *rubber*, your voice stays on all the way through.

L.say: A bride on a beach with a blue ribbon.

L.p: At the start of a stressed syllable, /p/ is followed by a strong puff of air (*pin*, *appear*). Hold your hand in front of your lips to feel it. After /s/ there is no puff: compare *pin* and *spin*.

L.say: Pass the peaches and the purple cups, please.

L.p: When a word finishes with /b/ or /p/, the sound itself can be hard to hear. Listen to the vowel instead: it is longer before /b/ (*cub*) and shorter before /p/ (*cup*).

L.say: Rob had a rib, but Rip had a cup.

L.tip: Korean speakers: at the start of a word, English listeners may hear your ㅂ as /p/, so *bin* can sound like *pin*. For /b/, think of the soft, voiced ㅂ in the middle of 아버지 and keep the puff of air for /p/ only. In final position, release the sound gently – don't swallow it, and don't add 으.

L.x: *subtle* has a silent *b*, so it is */ˈsʌtl/* (not */ˈsʌbtl/*).

L.p: /s/ and /z/ are made in the same place, with the air hissing through a narrow gap behind your top teeth. /s/ is voiceless; /z/ is voiced. In spelling, the letter *s* can be either, so you need to learn which.
It is spelt *s*, *ss*, *c* before *e*, *i* or *y* (*advice*, *circle*) and *sc* (*science*). Note that *s* between vowels is usually /z/, but not always: *basic* and *decide* have /s/.

L.say: I'd like a basic course in science, with some advice.

L.p: It is spelt *z*, but more often *s*: *design*, *result*, *reason*, *cousin*. *x* in *exam* and *exact* is /gz/.

L.say: My cousin's design won a prize for a thousand reasons.

L.p: In some pairs, the noun or adjective has /s/ and the verb has /z/: *use* (noun) /juːs/ and *use* (verb) /juːz/; *close* (near) /kləʊs/ and *close* (shut) /kləʊz/; *excuse* (noun) and *excuse* (verb). In *advice* and *advise*, the spelling changes too.

L.say: It's no use – I can't use it.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has no /z/, and ㅈ is a different sound. Make a long /s/ and switch on your voice – it should buzz. At the end of a word, /z/ often loses its buzz, so lengthen the vowel before it: *lose* has a longer vowel than *loose*.

L.x: *lose* ends with /z/, so it is */luːz/* (not */luːs/*), which is *loose*.

L.p: /d/ and /t/ are made with your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth. As with /b/ and /p/, the main difference at the start of a word is a puff of air after /t/; at the end of a word, it is the length of the vowel before them.
Release the tongue gently, with no puff of air. Between vowels, keep your voice on: *ladder*, *medal*.

L.say: The rider fed the dog in the garden.

L.p: Release the tongue with a puff of air at the start of a stressed syllable (*tight*, *attract*). Between vowels in British English, /t/ stays a clear /t/: *writer*, *metal*.

L.say: The writer bought a tight white metal box.

L.p: In careful British English, *writer* and *rider*, and *metal* and *medal*, sound different. In American English the /t/ between vowels becomes a quick /d/-like sound, so they can sound the same. Many British speakers replace /t/ with a tiny catch in the throat – a glottal stop – before a consonant or at the end of a word: *football*, *not now*, *get married*. Listen for it, but use a clear /t/ yourself between vowels.

L.say: I'm not sure – but it's not a bad idea.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean ㄷ at the start of a word can sound like /t/ to English ears, so *day* may be heard as *tay*. Think of the voiced ㄷ in the middle of 바다. At the end of a word, don't add 으 (*bed*, not 베드), and keep the vowel long before /d/: *ride* is longer than *right*.

L.x: *mortgage* has a silent *t*, so it is */ˈmɔːgɪdʒ/* (not */ˈmɔːtgɪdʒ/*).

L.p: /iː/ is long and tense, with spread lips; /e/ is short, with the mouth a little more open. The letters *ea* can spell either sound – *read* (now) is /riːd/, but *read* (past) is /red/ – so check each new *ea* word.
Spellings: *ee* (*wheel*), *ea* (*neat*), *e* (*complete*), *ei* after *c* (*receive*) and *ie* (*piece*).

L.say: Please keep a neat seat for the team leader.

L.p: Spellings: *e* (*set*), *ea* (*bread*, *weather*, *heavy*) and, in a few common words, *ai* (*said*) and *ie* (*friend*).

L.say: The weather was better, so we left the bread on the shelf.

L.p: Compare *feel* and *fell*, *cheek* and *check*, *beast* and *best*. Some pairs are noun and verb, or present and past: *breath* /breθ/ and *breathe* /briːð/, *read* /riːd/ and *read* /red/.

L.say: I read the news every day, and I read it yesterday too.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 에 is a good /e/, so the challenge is /iː/. Make it longer and tenser than 이, with your lips spread – *feel* should last noticeably longer than *fell*.

L.x: The past of *read* is said like *red*: */red/* (not */riːd/*).

L.p: Words with more than one syllable always contain a weak one. Weak syllables are short and quiet, and they nearly always use one of two weak vowels: /ə/ (the most common sound in English) or /ɪ/. Using them is what makes English words sound natural.

L.h: A /ə/ in the weak syllable, as in "sofa"

L.p: /ə/ can be spelt with any vowel letter. It is very common in endings such as *-er*, *-or*, *-ar*, *-our*, *-ure*, *-ous*, *-ant*, *-ent* and *-land*, and in beginnings such as *a-*, *con-* and *for-*.

L.say: The pilot from Poland lost control of the parrot.

L.h: B /ɪ/ in the weak syllable, as in "message"

L.p: /ɪ/ is common in endings such as *-age*, *-ed*, *-es*, *-est*, *-ic*, *-et* and *-ive*, and in beginnings such as *be-*, *de-*, *re-* and *e-*.

L.say: The biggest package of music tickets is damaged.

L.p: The two weak vowels are close, but they can separate words: *accept* /əkˈsept/ and *except* /ɪkˈsept/, *affect* /əˈfekt/ and *effect* /ɪˈfekt/.

L.say: Everyone accepted the invitation, except Tom.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 바나나 gives every vowel its full value, but English weak vowels are short, quiet and lazy. Don't pronounce the letters – *London* is /ˈlʌndən/, not 런던 with two equal syllables.

L.x: The weak syllable in *London* has /ə/: */ˈlʌndən/* (not */ˈlʌndɒn/*).

L.p: /f/ and /v/ are made with your top teeth resting lightly on your lower lip. /f/ is just air; /v/ adds your voice. Several English nouns end in /f/ while the matching verb ends in /v/.
Spellings: *f* and *ff* (*off*), *ph* (*graph*) and *gh* (*cough*, *laughter*).

L.say: I believe there's no proof of a fault in the ferry.

L.p: It is nearly always spelt *v*. The only common exception is *of* /əv/ – and *Stephen* /ˈstiːvn/.

L.say: Clever Vera avoided the vast, level valley.

L.p: Compare *belief* and *believe*, *proof* and *prove*, *relief* and *relieve*, *grief* and *grieve*, *half* and *halve*.

L.say: I can't believe it – what a relief!

L.tip: Korean speakers: without the teeth on the lip, /f/ turns into ㅍ and /v/ into ㅂ, so *ferry* becomes *Perry* and *vast* becomes *bast*. Some speakers also use ㅎ for /f/ (화이팅). Look in a mirror: you should see your top teeth on your lower lip for every /f/ and /v/.

L.x: *Stephen* has /v/ in the middle: */ˈstiːvn/* (not */ˈstefən/*).

L.p: /g/ and /k/ are made at the back of the mouth, with the back of your tongue against the soft palate. As with /b/–/p/ and /d/–/t/, the main clue is a puff of air after /k/ at the start of a stressed syllable, and a longer vowel before /g/ at the end of a word.
Spellings: *g* and *gg*, *gu* (*guest*, *guide*), *gh* (*ghost*) and *x* as /gz/ (*exam*). *g* is silent in *sign*, *design* and *foreign*.

L.say: Our guide said the ghost of a guard guards the gate.

L.p: Spellings: *c* and *k*, *ck*, *ch* (*character*, *chemistry*, *ache*), *que* (*unique*, *technique*) and *x* as /ks/. *k* is silent before *n*: *knee*, *knowledge*.

L.say: Kate's unique technique cured the ache in her ankle.

L.p: Compare *glass* and *class*, *angle* and *ankle*, *league* and *leak*.

L.say: Mind the gap, and don't drop your cap!

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean ㄱ at the start of a word may sound like /k/ to English ears, so *goal* can be heard as *coal*. Use the voiced ㄱ from the middle of 아기 for /g/, and keep a strong puff for /k/. At the end of a word, let the sound go gently instead of swallowing it: *bag* and *back* should not both sound like 백.

L.x: *sign* has a silent *g*, so it is */saɪn/* (not */saɪgn/*).

L.p: /h/, /w/ and /j/ only come before a vowel. /h/ is breath, /w/ starts with round lips, like a quick /uː/, and /j/ starts with the tongue high at the front, like a quick /iː/. Each one changes the word: *heat*, *wheat*, *eat*; *hello*, *yellow*.

/h/ is spelt *h* or *wh* (*who*, *whole*). It is silent in *hour*, *honest*, *heir*, *vehicle* and *exhausted*. In small words such as *him*, *her*, *his* and *have*, it often disappears in fast speech (see Unit 34).

L.say: Perhaps he'll behave himself ahead of the holidays.

L.p: /w/ is spelt *w*, *wh* (*when*, *why*), the *u* in *qu* (*quiet*) and the *o* in *one*.

L.say: Why was the quiet whale twenty miles away?

L.p: /j/ is spelt *y* (*yawn*), and it is hidden in many words with *u*, *ew* and *eu*: *use*, *new*, *beautiful*. It is even hidden in *onion* /ˈʌnjən/.

L.say: On Tuesday the new yellow yogurt was beautiful.

L.!: British English keeps a /j/ in *new*, *Tuesday*, *student* and *duty*: /njuː/, /ˈtjuːzdeɪ/. Most Americans say /nuː/, /ˈtuːzdeɪ/. Many British speakers also turn /tj/ and /dj/ into /tʃ/ and /dʒ/: /ˈtʃuːzdeɪ/, /ˈdʒuːti/.

L.tip: Korean speakers: there is no 우 or 이 with a glide in front, so *woman* can become 우먼, *wood* 우드, and *year* sounds like *ear*. Round your lips before *woman* and *would*, and start *year* and *yeast* with a quick /iː/.

L.x: *honest* has a silent *h*, so it is */ˈɒnɪst/* (not */ˈhɒnɪst/*).

L.p: /aɪ/ is a diphthong that glides from an open /a/ up to /ɪ/; /ɪ/ is a short vowel that stays still. Both are spelt with *i* or *y*, so learning the spelling patterns helps a lot.
Spellings: *i* + consonant + *e* (*bite*), *igh* (*sight*), *y* at the end of a word (*try*), and often *i* before *-nd* or *-ld* (*kind*, *wild*).

L.say: It's quite a nice, lively night for a bike ride.

L.p: Spellings: *i* before a final consonant or a double consonant (*bit*, *bitten*), and *y* in the middle of a word (*gym*, *myth*, *rhythm*). Note *build* and *women* too.

L.say: The children hid in the gym to get rid of him.

L.p: A few words change their vowel with their meaning: *wind* (air) /wɪnd/ but *wind* (turn) /waɪnd/; *live* (verb) /lɪv/ but *live* (adjective, as in *live music*) /laɪv/. And *child* has /aɪ/, but *children* has /ɪ/.

L.say: Where do you live? Do you like live music?

L.tip: Korean speakers: 아이 is two syllables in Korean, but /aɪ/ is one syllable that slides. Don't stretch the /ɪ/ in *bit* either – keep it short and loose, a little towards 에.

L.x: In *a live concert*, *live* is an adjective, so it is */laɪv/* (not */lɪv/*).

L.p: These three sounds are all made with the tongue just behind the ridge, and the lips pushed forward a little. /ʃ/ is a continuous hiss; /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ start with a stop, like /t/ or /d/, and then let the air out. /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ are voiceless; /dʒ/ is voiced.
Spellings: *sh*, *ti* and *ci* before a vowel (*nation*, *special*), *ch* in words from French (*chef*, *brochure*) and *s* in *sure* and *sugar*.

L.say: The chef shares a special brochure.

L.p: Spellings: *j*, *g* before *e*, *i* or *y* (*energy*, *religion*, *giant*), *dge* (*judge*) and *di* or *du* before a vowel (*soldier*, *education*).

L.say: The giant judge drank orange juice with the manager.

L.p: Spellings: *ch*, *tch* (*catch*) and *t* before *-ure* or *-ion* (*nature*, *question*).

L.say: Choose a chair and catch the question.

L.p: Compare *shoes* and *choose*, *wash* and *watch*, *cash* and *catch*, *chin* and *gin*.

L.say: Wash the dishes, then watch the match.

L.!: British English says *schedule* with /ʃ/: /ˈʃedjuːl/. American English says /ˈskedʒuːl/.

L.tip: Korean speakers: ㅊ is a good /tʃ/ and ㅈ (between vowels) is close to /dʒ/. For /ʃ/, push your lips forward and let the air flow without a stop – *share* starts with a hiss, *chair* with a small explosion. Keep /dʒ/ apart from /z/, too: *jail* is not *Zale*.

L.x: *chef* begins with /ʃ/, so it is */ʃef/* (not */tʃef/*).

L.p: English /l/ and /r/ are completely different sounds, but they can both feel like ㄹ to a Korean speaker. The key is the tongue: for /l/ it touches the ridge behind your top teeth; for /r/ it touches nothing.
Press your tongue tip on the ridge and let the air flow round the sides. /l/ sounds clear and bright before a vowel, and darker when it finishes a word (*fill*, *bottle*).

L.say: A loyal clown climbed the lane with a lamb.

L.p: Curl your tongue tip up and back without touching anything, and round your lips a little. In British English you only say /r/ before a vowel – *river*, but not *far* or *hard* – unless the next word starts with a vowel: *far away*.

L.say: The crown was a fright in the rain by the river.

L.p: The difference matters most after another consonant, where you have very little time: *flight* and *fright*, *blush* and *brush*, *clown* and *crown*. Get your tongue ready for the /l/ or /r/ while you say the first consonant.

L.say: The flight gave me a fright.

L.tip: Korean speakers: practise with a mirror. For /l/, you should see your tongue tip touching behind your top teeth. For /r/, you shouldn't see your tongue at all, and your lips should be slightly rounded. Start /r/ words with a short 우 to help: 우-*red*.

L.x: In British English *girl* has no /r/ sound: */gɜːl/* (not */gɜːrl/*).

L.p: /ɑː/ and /eə/ are both long, and in British English both are often spelt with an *r* that you do not pronounce. /ɑː/ stays still at the back of an open mouth; /eə/ starts at the front with /e/ and may move towards /ə/.
Spellings: *ar* (*star*, *sharp*), *al* (*calm*), *ear* (*heart*), *au* in *aunt*, and *a* before many consonant groups in British English (*dance*, *fast*, *after*).

L.say: My aunt and her partner danced under the stars.

L.p: Spellings: *air* (*fair*), *are* (*spare*, *scare*), *ear* (*bear*, *wear*), *ere* (*there*), *eir* (*their*) and *ar* before a vowel (*parent*, *various*).

L.say: My parents rarely prepare for various repairs.

L.p: In British English, the *r* in *star* and *fair* is silent – but it comes back when the next word starts with a vowel: *a star of the show* /ə ˈstɑːr əv ðə ˈʃəʊ/, *fair enough* /ˌfeər ɪˈnʌf/.

L.say: Fair enough – the star of the show is far away.

L.!: British English keeps *Mary* /ˈmeəri/, *marry* /ˈmæri/ and *merry* /ˈmeri/ apart; for many Americans they all sound the same.

L.tip: Korean speakers: hold /ɑː/ long and open, like a long 아. /eə/ is like 에어 said as one smooth syllable – and leave out the r in both, unless a vowel follows.

L.x: In British English *aunt* has the vowel of *car*: */ɑːnt/* (not */ænt/*).

L.p: /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/ are nasal sounds: the air comes out through your nose. They are made in the same three places as /b/, /d/ and /g/ – the lips, the ridge and the back of the mouth.
Lips closed. It is spelt *m*, *mm*, *mb* (*thumb*) and *mn* (*autumn*, *column*), where the second letter is silent.

L.say: I dream of a calm autumn by the sea.

L.p: Tongue tip on the ridge. In words like *button*, *sudden* and *listen*, /n/ makes a syllable by itself, with no vowel: /ˈbʌtn/.

L.say: None of us ran in the sudden rain.

L.p: Back of the tongue up, as for /g/. Spelt *ng*, or *n* before /k/ (*uncle*). There is no /g/ after /ŋ/ at the end of a word (*thing*), or in words made from it (*singer*), but there is in comparatives (*longer*, *stronger*, *younger*) and in *finger*, *hungry* and *English*.

L.say: My younger uncle is stronger than a singer.

L.p: In fast speech /n/ often copies the next sound: *ten pounds* sounds like /tem paʊndz/, and *in Kent* like /ɪŋ kent/. You will practise this in Unit 40.

L.!: In casual speech, many British people say *-ing* as /ɪn/: *goin'*, *somethin'*. It is informal – say /ɪŋ/ yourself.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 밤, 반 and 방 show that you already have all three sounds. The difficulties are adding a /g/ after /ŋ/ (*singer*, not 씽거) and leaving it out where English has one (*longer* /ˈlɒŋgə/).

L.x: *autumn* has a silent *n*, so it is */ˈɔːtəm/* (not */ˈɔːtəmn/*).

L.p: /əʊ/ is a diphthong: it starts in the centre of the mouth and glides to /ʊ/ as the lips round. /ɒ/ is a short vowel made with the mouth open and the lips slightly rounded – and it stays still. In British English the two are very different; mixing them up can turn *won't* into *want*.
Spellings: *o* + consonant + *e* (*woke*), *oa* (*road*), *ow* (*known*), *o* before *-ld*, *-st* or at the end of a word (*cold*, *most*, *go*), and *ou* or *ough* (*soul*, *though*).

L.say: I won't go home alone on the cold road.

L.p: Spellings: *o* before a final consonant or a double consonant (*got*, *cotton*), *a* after *w* or *qu* (*want*, *swan*, *quality*), and *au* or *ou* in a few words (*sausage*, *because*, *cough*).

L.say: What a lot of hot sausages in a wok!

L.p: *know* is /nəʊ/, but *knowledge* is /ˈnɒlɪdʒ/. *though* has /əʊ/, but *cough* has /ɒ/. Learn these words with their sounds.

L.!: The British /ɒ/ is short and rounded. In American English, words such as *hot*, *stop* and *got* have an unrounded vowel much closer to the /ɑː/ of *car*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: if you say 오 for both sounds, *coat* and *cot* will be the same. For /əʊ/, start from a relaxed 어 and glide to 우 (*coat* is close to a quick 커우트). For /ɒ/, open your mouth more and keep it short and still.

L.x: *knowledge* has the vowel of *hot*: */ˈnɒlɪdʒ/* (not */ˈnəʊlɪdʒ/*), even though *know* is /nəʊ/.

L.p: Both *th* sounds are made with the tongue tip lightly between or just behind the top teeth. /θ/ is voiceless; /ð/ is voiced. Some pairs of related words change from one to the other: *breath* and *breathe*, *north* and *northern*.
/θ/ is found in most nouns, verbs and adjectives with *th*: *thank*, *thought*, *method*, *healthy*.

L.say: The author thought the healthy method was worth a theory.

L.p: /ð/ is found in small grammar words (*the*, *this*, *than*, *although*) and in the middle of many words (*rather*, *either*). Verbs made from *th* nouns often end in /ð/: *breathe*, *clothe*, *bathe*.

L.say: Although it was rather cold in the northern hills, we bathed in the river.

L.p: Compare *breath* and *breathe*, *cloth* and *clothe*, *bath* /bɑːθ/ and *bathe* /beɪð/, *north* and *northern*, *south* /saʊθ/ and *southern* /ˈsʌðən/, *worth* and *worthy*.

L.say: Take a deep breath and breathe slowly.

L.!: In some British accents, especially in London, *th* is said as /f/ or /v/ (*free* for *three*, *bruvver* for *brother*). It is very common, but it is not the standard model. A few names spelt *th* have /t/: *Thomas*, *Thames*, *Thailand*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: if /θ/ becomes ㅆ, *thought* sounds like *sought*; if /ð/ becomes ㄷ, *although* sounds like 올도. Let your tongue touch your top teeth for every *th* – and practise the small words (*the*, *that*, *than*) most, because they are everywhere.

L.x: *Thailand* begins with /t/, so it is */ˈtaɪlænd/* (not */ˈθaɪlænd/*).

L.p: These three vowels are all made with the tongue at the back of the mouth, and the spelling *oo* can be any of them: *blood* /ʌ/, *book* /ʊ/, *food* /uː/. /ʌ/ is short with unrounded lips; /ʊ/ is short with loosely rounded lips; /uː/ is long, with tight, rounded lips.
Spellings: *u* (*luck*), *o* (*honey*, *oven*, *wonder*), *ou* (*touch*, *double*) and *oo* in *blood* and *flood*.

L.say: Good luck – my honey cake is still in the oven.

L.p: Spellings: *oo* (*look*, *wooden*), *u* (*put*, *pudding*, *butcher*), *ou* in *could*, *would* and *should*, and *o* in *woman* and *wolf*.

L.say: The butcher stood by the wooden pudding.

L.p: Spellings: *oo* (*food*), *u* + consonant + *e* (*rule*), *ue*, *ew* (*chew*), *ou* (*group*, *route*), *ui* (*fruit*) and *o* (*move*, *improve*).

L.say: Luke's group moved to a new school route.

L.p: Compare *luck*, *look* and *Luke*; *tuck* and *took*; *full* and *fool*.

L.say: Look, Luke – good luck!

L.tip: Korean speakers: 어 is close to /ʌ/ and 우 is close to /uː/, but /ʊ/ sits between them – relaxed lips, a short sound. Many learners say *look* with a long 우 (루크): keep it short.

L.x: *butcher* has /ʊ/, so it is */ˈbʊtʃə/* (not */ˈbʌtʃə/*).

L.p: /ɜː/ and /ɔː/ are both long, and in British English both are often spelt with an *r* that you don't pronounce. /ɜː/ is made in the middle of the mouth with flat, relaxed lips; /ɔː/ is made at the back with round lips.
Spellings: *er*, *ir*, *ur*, *ear* (*learn*, *pearl*), *or* after *w* (*word*, *work*) and *our* in *journey*.

L.say: The first bird I heard was a pearl of a journey.

L.p: Spellings: *or*, *ore*, *oar* (*board*), *our* (*course*, *pour*), *aw* (*lawn*), *au*, *al* (*walk*) and *ar* after *w* or *qu* (*war*, *reward*, *quarter*).

L.say: Paul poured water on the lawn for a quarter of an hour.

L.p: Compare *firm* and *form*, *word* and *ward*, *were* and *war*, *learn* and *lawn*. Flat lips: /ɜː/. Round lips: /ɔː/.

L.say: We were at war with words.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has nothing like /ɜː/, so it often becomes 어 or 오 – and *work* turns into *walk*, *were* into *war*. Keep your lips flat and spread for /ɜː/, and hold it long, like a long, relaxed 어 with no rounding.

L.x: *journey* has /ɜː/, so it is */ˈdʒɜːni/* (not */ˈdʒɔːni/*).

L.p: /ɔɪ/ and /aʊ/ are both diphthongs, but they move in opposite directions. /ɔɪ/ starts with round lips and glides forward to /ɪ/; /aʊ/ starts wide open and glides back to /ʊ/, rounding the lips at the end.
It is spelt *oi* (*foil*, *joint*, *poison*) or *oy* (*royal*, *destroy*).

L.say: The royal employer avoided the poison in the moist foil.

L.p: It is spelt *ow* (*allow*, *drown*) or *ou* (*shout*, *mountain*, *account*, *county*).

L.say: How loud the crowd shouted on the mountain!

L.p: *bow* and *row* each have two pronunciations. *bow* is /baʊ/ when you bend at the waist, but /bəʊ/ for a ribbon or the weapon for arrows. *row* is /raʊ/ for an argument, but /rəʊ/ for a line of seats or moving a boat.

L.say: After the row, they sat in the back row.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 오이 and 아우 are two syllables in Korean, but /ɔɪ/ and /aʊ/ are one syllable each. Keep the glide smooth and quick: *coin* is one beat, not 코-인.

L.x: *row* meaning an argument rhymes with *cow*: */raʊ/* (not */rəʊ/*).

L.p: A syllable is one beat of speech, built round one vowel sound. Adding consonants does not add syllables: *ate*, *eight*, *great* and *straight* all have one syllable, although the last has five letters before the vowel sound ends. Only vowel sounds make new beats.
English allows many consonants round a single vowel, so long words on paper can be short in speech: *strengths*, *scratched*, *crisps*.

In everyday speech some words lose a weak vowel, and with it a syllable: *every* /ˈevri/, *different* /ˈdɪfrənt/, *camera* /ˈkæmrə/, *chocolate* /ˈtʃɒklət/, *temperature* /ˈtemprətʃə/. And a few syllables have no vowel at all: in *little*, *bottle* and *button* the /l/ or /n/ makes the beat by itself.

L.say: Every different camera has a little button.

L.tip: Korean speakers: a Korean syllable usually has one vowel and at most one final consonant, so English loanwords grow extra syllables – 스트렝스 for *strength*. Clap while you say English words, and count only the vowel sounds.

L.x: *strength* has one syllable, so it is */streŋθ/* (not */səˈtreŋθ/*).

L.p: In every word of more than one syllable, one syllable is stressed: it is longer, louder and a little higher, and it has a full vowel. The other syllables are weaker, and often have /ə/ or /ɪ/. Dictionaries mark the stressed syllable with /ˈ/; this course also shows the pattern with circles, such as *Ooo*.

The stress often moves between a country and its people or language: *ITaly* but *iTALian*, *CANada* but *caNAdian*, *JaPAN* but *JapaNESE*, *EGypt* but *eGYPtian*. Learn each pair as two separate words.

L.say: Italy and Italian, Japan and Japanese.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean loanwords give every syllable the same weight, so 이탈리아 has four equal beats. In *Italy* only the first syllable is strong, and in *Italian* only the second. Getting the stress right is often more important for being understood than getting every sound right.

L.x: *Japanese* is stressed on the last syllable, so it is */ˌdʒæpəˈniːz/* (not */dʒəˈpæniːz/*).

L.p: In a sentence, the words that carry the meaning are stressed and the grammar words are not. If you heard only the stressed words – *MEET me at the STAtion at SIX* – you would still understand the message. English rhythm is built on these stressed syllables, which come at fairly regular intervals.
A short phrase can have exactly the same rhythm as a word: *a boat* sounds like *about*, and *to stay* like *today*.

L.h: Words or phrases – the same beat

L.p: Because grammar words are weak, *I've met her* has the rhythm of *remember*, and *on the phone* has the rhythm of *afternoon*. Thinking in rhythm patterns, not words, helps you sound natural and helps you hear fast speech.

L.say: I've met her. Remember? On the phone, this afternoon.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean timing gives each syllable a similar length. In English, the unstressed words between the beats are squeezed: *at the* in *at the station* is very short. Tap the beats with your finger and fit the small words in between them.

L.x: In *on the phone*, *on* and *the* are weak, so it sounds like */ɒn ðə ˈfəʊn/* (not */ˈɒn ˈðiː ˈfəʊn/*).

L.p: English syllables can start with up to three consonants. Say the whole group quickly and smoothly, with no vowel before it or between the consonants: *strange* has one syllable, not three.
Common groups: a consonant + /l/ or /r/ (*brick*, *slow*), /s/ + a consonant (*smoke*), and a consonant + /w/ (*twin*, *queen*, *dwell*).

L.say: The queen's twin threw a brick at the smoke.

L.h: B a consonant + a hidden /j/, as in "music"

L.p: Many words spelt with *u* or *ew* start with a consonant and a /j/: *huge* /hjuːdʒ/, *view* /vjuː/, *beauty* /ˈbjuːti/. The /j/ is not in the spelling, but it is part of the group.

L.say: The huge view of the pure blue sea was a beauty.

L.p: Three-consonant groups always start with /s/: /spr/, /str/, /skr/, /spl/, /skw/ – and, in British English, /stj/ in *stew* and *student*.

L.say: Squeeze the strange spray and splash the screen.

L.h: When a vowel changes the word

L.p: Adding a vowel to a group can make a different word: *claps* and *collapse*, *plight* and *polite*, *drive* and *derive*.

L.say: The audience claps. The building collapses.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 스, 트 and 프 in loanwords each add a syllable, so *street* becomes 스트리트. Try whispering the first consonants and saying only the vowel aloud: *s-t-r-EET*. Then join them.

L.x: *strength* has no vowel before or inside the first group, so it is */streŋθ/* (not */səˈtreŋθ/*).

L.p: Syllables can also end with several consonants – up to four in words like *texts* and *sixths*. Adding endings such as *-s*, *-ed* and *-th* makes many of these groups: *pay*, *paint*, *paints* are all one syllable.

L.h: A two consonants at the end, as in "paint"

C four consonants at the end, as in "texts"

L.p: When three or four consonants come together, native speakers often drop one from the middle: *texts* can sound like /teks/, *asked* like /ɑːst/ and *months* like /mʌns/. Listen out for this – and say the full group yourself when you speak carefully.

L.say: She asked for the facts in six texts.

L.tip: Korean speakers: a Korean syllable ends in one consonant at most, so an English group often loses its last sounds or gains an extra vowel: *gifts* becomes 기프트 or *gif*. The last consonant often carries grammar (*-s*, *-ed*), so make sure it is there.

L.x: *asked* ends in /skt/, so it is */ɑːskt/* (not */ˈɑːskɪd/*).

L.p: The ending *-s* (plurals, verbs with *he/she/it*, possessives) and the short forms *'s* (*is*, *has*) are usually just a consonant added to the syllable – /s/ or /z/. Only after a hissing or hushing sound does the ending become a new syllable, /ɪz/.
After a voiceless consonant: *lifts*, *tastes*, *jumps*, *myths*.

After a vowel or a voiced consonant: *goes*, *knives*, *leaves*. Note that some plurals change the last sound of the word as well: *knife* /naɪf/ but *knives* /naɪvz/; *bath* /bɑːθ/ but *baths* /bɑːðz/; *path*, *paths*; *mouth*, *mouths*.
After /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/ or /dʒ/ the ending adds a syllable: *wishes*, *judges*, *garages*. *house* /haʊs/ changes too: *houses* /ˈhaʊzɪz/.
After a hissing or hushing sound, *is* stays a separate syllable: *The bus is late* /ðə ˈbʌs ɪz ˈleɪt/. After other sounds it joins the word before as *'s*: *The train's late*.

L.say: The bus is late, but the train's on time.

L.tip: Korean speakers: the -s ending is small, but it carries grammar – *my friend spends* and *my friends spend* mean different things. Make it clear, and don't add a vowel after it: *lifts* is one syllable.

L.x: *houses* changes /s/ to /z/, so it is */ˈhaʊzɪz/* (not */ˈhaʊsɪz/*).

L.p: The *-ed* ending is usually just a consonant, /t/ or /d/, added to the last syllable. It only adds a syllable, /ɪd/, after /t/ or /d/. So *walked* has one syllable, and *wanted* has two.
After a voiceless sound: *dressed*, *reached*, *coughed*, *relaxed*, *finished*.
After a vowel or a voiced sound: *robbed*, *begged*, *breathed*, *followed*, *remembered*.
After /t/ or /d/: *counted*, *landed*, *invited*. A few adjectives ending in *-ed* also have /ɪd/, even after other sounds: *naked*, *wicked*, *crooked* (bent), *rugged*.

Before another consonant, a /t/ or /d/ ending is often hard to hear: *I walked to work* can sound like *I walk to work*. Listen for the time words – *yesterday*, *last week* – and for the past tense in the rest of the sentence.

L.say: We walked to the station, waited and arrived late.

L.tip: Korean speakers: the most common mistake is an extra syllable – *finished* as 피니시드. Only /t/ and /d/ verbs get one. Say *finished* as two syllables: /ˈfɪnɪʃt/.

L.p: Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the first syllable (*Oo*), and most two-syllable verbs on the second (*oO*). That is a tendency, not a rule – but it explains an interesting group of words that can be either a noun or a verb.
Nouns and adjectives such as *mirror*, *garlic* and *modern*, and some verbs: *answer*, *promise*, *follow*, *worry*.
Verbs such as *prefer*, *admit* and *deny*, and some nouns: *canal*, *cartoon*, *event*.

In some words the spelling stays the same, but the stress moves: a *REcord* but to *reCORD*; a *PREsent* but to *preSENT*; an *OBject* but to *obJECT*; an *INcrease* but to *inCREASE*; a *SUSpect* but to *susPECT*. The vowels change too: the stressed one is full, and the other one becomes weak – *record* (noun) /ˈrekɔːd/, *record* (verb) /rɪˈkɔːd/.

L.say: She wants to record a new world record.
They will present her with a present.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean words do not change meaning with stress, so it is easy to ignore. In English, *a DEsert* (sand) and *to deSERT* (leave) are different words. When you learn a word that can be a noun and a verb, learn its two stress patterns too.

L.x: *hotel* is a noun, but it is stressed on the second syllable: */həʊˈtel/* (not */ˈhəʊtel/*).

L.p: A compound is two words used as one: *greenhouse*, *bus station*, *washing machine*. Most compound nouns are stressed on the first part. But an adjective + noun that is not a compound – a *green house*, a house that is green – is stressed on the second part. So stress can tell you which one is meant.

L.h: A first part stressed, as in "BUS stop"

L.p: Compound nouns, including nouns made from phrasal verbs: a *BREAKdown*, a *TAKEaway*, a *CHECK-in*.

L.say: The car had a breakdown near the bus station.

L.h: B second part stressed, as in "brand-NEW"

L.p: Adjective + noun phrases (*a green HOUSE*), compound adjectives (*bad-TEMpered*, *home-MADE*) and phrasal verbs (*break DOWN*, *check IN*).

L.say: The car broke down near the green house.

L.p: *a DARKroom* is a room for developing photos; *a dark ROOM* is any room with no light. *a BLACKbird* is a kind of bird; *a black BIRD* is any bird that is black. *an ENGlish teacher* teaches English; *an English TEACHer* comes from England.

L.say: An English teacher? Yes – but she's Scottish.

L.!: Place names follow patterns too: *BUS station*, *POST office*, but *town HALL*; *OXford Street*, but *Oxford ROAD*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when two words make one idea, say them as one word with one strong beat at the start: *WASHing machine*, not *washing MAchine*. Saving the strong beat for the first part also tells the listener that it is one thing.

L.x: *washing machine* is a compound noun, so it is stressed on *washing*: *WASHing machine* (not *washing maCHINE*).

L.p: Many long words are made from a shorter word plus a beginning (prefix) or an ending (suffix). With most prefixes and many suffixes the stress stays where it was in the shorter word: *HAPpy*, *unHAPpy*, *unHAPpiness*.
Endings such as *-ful*, *-ness*, *-ment*, *-ly* and *-less* do not move the stress: *CAREful*, *CAREfully*, *CARElessness*.
Beginnings such as *un-*, *dis-*, *in-*, *mis-* and *re-* do not take the stress: *unLUCKy*, *disHONest*.
Add both, and the stress still stays put: *unCOMfortable*, *unFORtunate*, *forGETfulness*.

L.say: I was unhappy and uncomfortable, but everyone was so helpful.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when you learn a long word, find the short word inside it and keep its stress. *unfortunately* is hard to say until you notice *FORtunate* inside it: *unFORtunately*.

L.p: Some endings do move the stress. With *-ic*, *-ical*, *-ity*, *-ion*, *-ian* and *-ial*, the stress falls on the syllable just before the ending – wherever it was before: *PHOtograph*, *phoTOgraphy*, *photoGRAPHic*.

Learn word families together, and listen to the stress jump: *POlitics*, *poLItical*, *poliTIcian*; *DEmocrat*, *deMOcracy*, *demoCRAtic*; *HIStory*, *hisTORic*, *hisTORical*. The vowels change as well – a vowel is full when it is stressed and weak when it is not.

L.say: Politics, political, politician. Democrat, democracy, democratic.

L.tip: Korean speakers: these families are common in academic and news English. If you keep the stress of the short word – *POlitician* – listeners may not recognise the word at all. Mark the stress whenever you write a new word in your notes.

L.x: *photography* moves the stress, so it is */fəˈtɒgrəfi/* (not */ˈfəʊtəgrɑːfi/*).

L.p: Normally, small grammar words are weak. But some short phrases are made only of meaning words – signs, warnings and short messages – and then every word is stressed. Each word is said clearly and separately, and the last one is the strongest.
*WET PAINT*, *STAFF ONLY*, *NO PARKING*: each word gets a beat, with the main stress on the last.
Warnings, wishes and orders are often like this too: *GOOD LUCK!*, *TAKE CARE!*, *LAST ORDERS!*

L.h: When a small word gets in

L.p: If a grammar word is part of the phrase, it is weak, even here: *OUT of ORder*, *MIND the GAP*, *KEEP off the GRASS*.

L.say: Wet paint. Staff only. Out of order. Mind the gap.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when every word is stressed, slow down and give each word its own beat, with a little extra weight on the last one. *Good luck!* said quickly and flatly can sound careless; said clearly, it sounds warm.

L.p: Grammar words – articles, pronouns, prepositions, helping verbs and words like *that*, *some* and *and* – are usually unstressed. They are said quickly and quietly, often with /ə/, and they squeeze in between the stressed words. Some of them have a strong and a weak form that do different jobs.

L.h: A that /ðət/, joining two parts of a sentence

L.p: When *that* introduces a clause – *I think that…*, *the film that I saw* – it is weak: /ðət/.
When *that* points to something – *that one*, *Look at that!* – it is strong: /ðæt/.
When *some* means "an amount of", it is weak: *some milk* /səm ˈmɪlk/.

L.h: D some /sʌm/, certain ones but not others

L.p: When *some* means "certain ones, but not all", it is strong: *SOME people agree*.

L.say: I think that that one's better. Some people like some milk in their tea.

L.tip: Korean speakers: listening is where weak forms matter most. If you expect to hear every word clearly, fast English seems to have words missing. Expect the small words to be quick and blurred – and try saying them that way yourself.

L.x: In *I'm sure that he's right*, *that* is weak: */ðət/* (not */ðæt/*).

L.p: Pronouns are normally unstressed, and in fast speech many of them lose sounds. *him*, *her*, *his* and *he* often lose their /h/ in the middle of a sentence, and *them* can become /ðəm/ or even /əm/. Joined to the word before, they can sound like part of it: *meet her* sounds just like *metre*, and *call him* like the name *Callum*.

L.h: A him /ɪm/, his /ɪz/ and he /i/ with no /h/

L.p: Helping verbs after a pronoun are usually contracted: *I'll*, *she'd*, *we've*. Even *it will* becomes *it'll* /ˈɪtl/. In very fast speech you may hear two contractions together: *I'd've* /ˈaɪdəv/ (I would have).
The difference between *I go* and *I'll go*, or *I like* and *I'd like*, is often just a short /l/ or /d/ – but it changes the meaning. Listen for it carefully.

L.say: I'll call him tonight, and I'd like to meet her too.

L.tip: Korean speakers: if you say *her* as a full 허 every time, your English will sound slow and heavy – and you may miss it when others say it. Practise *tell her*, *ask her*, *meet her* as one word: *teller*, *asker*, *metre*.

L.x: In *I'll ask her*, *her* is weak: */ˈɑːsk ə/* (not */ˈɑːsk hɜː/*).

L.p: The verb *be* is usually unstressed. *am*, *is* and *are* are contracted after pronouns (*I'm*, *it's*, *they're*) and often after nouns too (*the food's good*). *was* and *were* have weak forms, /wəz/ and /wə/, and so does *been*: /bɪn/. They are only strong in short answers, in negatives, at the end of a sentence or for emphasis.
Before a vowel, the silent *r* of *were* comes back: *they were out* /ðeɪ wər ˈaʊt/.

L.h: C is and are joined to a noun

L.p: After a noun, *is* is usually just /s/ or /z/, and *are* just /ə/: *the food's good*, *the kids are fine*. After a hissing sound, *is* stays a separate syllable (*the bus is late*) – see Unit 26.
In the middle of a sentence *been* is weak in British English: *I've been busy* /aɪv bɪn ˈbɪzi/. It is strong at the end: *Where have you been?* /biːn/.
Weak *was* and *were* can be hard to hear, so *It was fine* and *It's fine* may sound alike. Listen for the time words and the rest of the sentence.

L.say: They were out when we were there, but it was fine.

L.tip: Korean speakers: in your own speech, make *was* and *were* short and weak, but don't drop them – the tense is in the verb. When you listen, expect them to be quick and quiet.

L.x: In *I've been busy*, *been* is weak: */bɪn/* (not */biːn/*).

L.p: Helping verbs – *do*, *does*, *did*, *have*, *has*, *can*, *could*, *would*, *should* – are weak in most questions and statements. They are strong in short answers, in negatives, at the end of a sentence and when you stress them for emphasis.
In questions, *do you* is often just /də ju/ or even /djə/.

L.h: B have after could, should, would and must: /əv/

L.p: *could have*, *should have*, *would have* and *must have* are usually /ˈkʊdəv/, /ˈʃʊdəv/, /ˈwʊdəv/, /ˈmʌstəv/. That is why people sometimes wrongly write *should of* – but the correct spelling is always *should have* (or *should've*).

L.h: Weak in questions, strong in answers

L.p: A: *Can you swim?* /kən/ – B: *Yes, I can.* /kæn/. A: *Have you finished?* /həv/ – B: *Yes, I have.* /hæv/.

L.say: Do you like it? Yes, I do. Could you have done it? Yes, I could.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when you write down English you hear, the weak forms can trick you. If you hear /ˈʃʊdəv/, write *should have*. And when you speak, saying *do you* as 두 유 with two strong words makes questions sound slow and heavy.

L.x: In *Where do you live?*, *do* is weak: */də/* (not */duː/*).

L.p: Three of the most common words in English – *a*, *of* and *or* – can all sound like the same short /ə/. *of* is /əv/ before a vowel but often just /ə/ before a consonant; *or* is /ə/, with a linking /r/ before a vowel. So you have to understand them from the context.

L.say: Would you like a glass of milk or a cup of tea?

L.p: In connected speech there are no gaps between words. When a word ends with a consonant and the next word begins with a vowel, the consonant moves across and starts the next syllable: *look it up* sounds like *loo-ki-tup*. Hearing this helps you find where words begin and end.

L.h: A a consonant moves to the next word

L.say: Once upon a time, as a matter of fact, I filled it in.

L.p: Because the gaps disappear, some phrases sound alike: *grade A* and *grey day*, *that stuff* and *that's tough*, *ice cream* and *I scream*. In real speech, the meaning usually tells you which one you heard.

L.say: I scream for ice cream.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean does the same (옷이 is said 오시), so use the same habit in English. *turn it off* is *tur-ni-toff* – one smooth line, with no stop and no 으.

L.p: When one word ends with a vowel sound and the next begins with one, English joins them with a small extra sound, so the voice never stops. Which sound it is depends on the first vowel.

After /ɑː/, /ɔː/, /ɜː/, /ə/, /ɪə/ and /eə/, the silent British *r* comes back before a vowel: *here it is* /ˈhɪər ɪt ɪz/, *better off*. Many speakers add an /r/ even where there is no *r* in the spelling – *law and order* /ˌlɔːr ən ˈɔːdə/, *the idea of it* – so listen for it.
After /uː/, /əʊ/ and /aʊ/, a light /w/ joins the words: *go on* /ˌgəʊ ˈwɒn/, *how about*.
After /iː/, /ɪ/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/ and /ɔɪ/, a light /j/ joins the words: *be able* /ˌbiː ˈjeɪbl/, *my uncle*.

L.say: Here it is – go on, try it on, and see if it fits.

L.tip: Korean speakers: you don't need to make the linking sounds strong. Just keep your voice going and move smoothly from one vowel to the next – the /r/, /w/ or /j/ will appear by itself. Stopping between the vowels is what makes English sound choppy.

L.x: In British English *here it is* has a linking /r/: */ˈhɪər ɪt ɪz/* (not */ˈhɪə ɪt ɪz/* with a stop).

L.p: When two consonants meet across words, the first one often changes to be more like the second, or disappears. These changes are normal in fluent, careful British speech – and they are a big reason why fast English can be hard to understand.

L.h: A /n/ becomes /m/ or /ŋ/, as in "in Paris"

L.p: Before /p/, /b/ or /m/, /n/ becomes /m/: *ten pounds* /tem ˈpaʊndz/. Before /k/ or /g/, it becomes /ŋ/: *in Korea* /ɪŋ kəˈriːə/.

L.h: B /t/ and /d/ change, as in "white bread"

L.p: /t/ and /d/ often become /p/ and /b/ before /p/, /b/ and /m/ (*that boy* /ðæp ˈbɔɪ/, *good morning* /gʊb ˈmɔːnɪŋ/), and /k/ and /g/ before /k/ and /g/ (*that girl* /ðæk ˈgɜːl/).

L.h: C /t/ or /d/ + /j/ join, as in "would you"

L.p: /t/ + /j/ becomes /tʃ/ and /d/ + /j/ becomes /dʒ/: *don't you* /ˈdəʊntʃu/, *did you* /ˈdɪdʒu/.
Before /ʃ/ or /j/, /s/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/ becomes /ʒ/: *this shop* /ðɪʃ ˈʃɒp/, *this year* /ðɪʃ ˈjɪə/, *is she* /ɪʒ ʃi/.

L.say: Did you meet that boy in Korea this year? Good morning!

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has very similar rules – 신문 is said 심문 and 같이 is said 가치 – so these changes may feel natural. You don't have to make them yourself, but knowing them will help you understand fast speech, especially *did you*, *don't you* and *would you*.

L.x: In fast speech *ten pounds* usually sounds like */tem ˈpaʊndz/* (not */teŋ ˈpaʊndz/*).

L.p: Real conversation is fast. Small words are weak, words run together, and sounds change or disappear – everything you have practised in Units 33–40, all at once. Nobody hears every word perfectly, not even native speakers. Good listeners focus on the stressed words, use the situation to fill the gaps, and ask when they really need to.
Use a rising voice to show it is a question, and keep it friendly.
Repeat the part you are not sure about, with a rise: *Fifteen?* *Tomorrow?*

Common phrases are often squeezed together: *What are you doing?* can sound like /ˈwɒtʃə ˈduːɪŋ/, *I don't know* like /aɪ ˈdəʊnəʊ/, and *Let me see* like /ˈlemi ˈsiː/. Once you know these shapes, you hear them everywhere.

L.say: What are you doing later? I don't know – let me see.

L.tip: Korean speakers: it is completely normal to ask people to repeat or slow down, and English speakers expect it. Asking with a clear, rising "Sorry?" is far better than nodding and guessing.

L.p: When you read aloud, your voice has to do the work of the punctuation. Listeners cannot see the commas and full stops – they hear them as pauses and tunes.

L.h: Commas, full stops and question marks

L.p: A comma is a short pause, often with the voice level or rising: there's more to come. A full stop is a longer pause, with the voice falling. A question that you answer with *yes* or *no* usually rises; a question with *what*, *where* or *how* usually falls.

L.say: When we arrived, the hotel was closed. Was there another one nearby? Where could we go?

L.p: In a list, the voice rises on each item and falls on the last: *apples, pears, and grapes*. Words in brackets or between dashes are said a little faster and lower, like an aside. A colon is a pause before an explanation or a list.

L.say: We bought apples, pears and grapes – and a melon, which was far too heavy.

L.p: When you read someone's words, pause before them and change your voice slightly, so the listener knows who is speaking.

L.say: She looked at me and said, "I'm not going."

L.p: Some written forms are read as words: *e.g.* is *for example*, *i.e.* is *that is*, *etc.* is *et cetera*. Abbreviations are read as letters (*BBC*, *UK*) or as a word (*NATO*). Symbols are read in full: *£20* is *twenty pounds*, *10%* is *ten per cent*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when you read aloud, it is tempting to read every word at the same speed. Slow down, use the punctuation to plan your pauses, and let your voice fall clearly at each full stop – it makes you much easier to follow.

L.p: How you group words into chunks can change what a sentence means. The pauses and the stress show which words belong together.

*My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a teacher* – with pauses – means I have one brother, and he lives in Leeds. *My brother who lives in Leeds is a teacher* – with no pauses – means I have more than one brother, and I'm talking about the one in Leeds.

L.say: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a teacher. My brother who lives in Leeds is a teacher.

L.p: In the same way, *two plus three | times four* is 20, but *two | plus three times four* is 14. And *She dressed | and fed the baby* is different from *She dressed and fed the baby*.
Pairs of words that often go together are said as one chunk, with *and* very weak: *bread and butter* /ˌbred n ˈbʌtə/.

L.say: I'm sick and tired of the noise – I just want some peace and quiet.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean shows how words group with particles and endings. English uses pauses and stress instead, so a pause in the wrong place can change the meaning. When a sentence is important, group it carefully.

L.p: In conversation, a pause can be a signal that you have finished. If you need time to think but want to keep speaking, you have to show it – with hesitation sounds, with a level voice, and with phrases that hold your turn.

British speakers fill pauses with *er* /ɜː/ and *erm* /ɜːm/ (American speakers say *uh* and *um*), or with words like *well* and *let me think*. Say them with a level voice, not a fall, and stretch them a little.

L.say: Well… let me think… erm… I'd say it was about ten years ago.

L.p: Phrases such as *the thing is* and *what I mean is* tell the listener there is more to come. A stretched, level word does the same: *and…*, *so…*

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean fillers such as 음, 어 or 그… sound strange in English – and 그 can even be misheard. Swap them for *erm*, *well* or *let me think*, and keep your voice level so the other person waits for you.

L.p: Storytellers guide their listeners with signal words and with their voice. A new part of the story starts high; an aside drops lower and faster; and the voice slows down and pauses just before the important moment.
These openers get attention. Say them with a high, lively voice.

L.say: Guess what? Last night, all of a sudden, the lights went out. Anyway, to cut a long story short, it was the cat.

L.p: When you add some background in the middle of the story, drop your voice and speed up a little, then come back with *anyway*: *My neighbour – he's a firefighter, actually – came round. Anyway…*

L.tip: Korean speakers: in Korean, the flow of a story is often carried by endings such as -는데 and -거든. In English, the signal words and the voice do this job. Try telling a short story with a higher start for each new part, and a slow, quiet pause before the surprise.

L.p: Small talk is relaxed, friendly conversation, and it is full of vague language – words that make what we say less exact on purpose. They are said quickly and weakly, so they can be hard to hear: *sort of* often sounds like /ˈsɔːtə/, and *kind of* like /ˈkaɪndə/.
*sort of*, *kind of*, *a bit*, and the British ending *-ish*: *sevenish* (about seven o'clock), *greenish*, *tallish*.

L.h: B making a list less exact

L.p: *you know*, *I mean* and *like* give you time and make your speech sound relaxed. Use them sparingly – too many sound careless.

L.say: It was sort of greenish, you know, and quite big, and stuff like that.

L.tip: Korean speakers: vague language can sound careless if you say it slowly and clearly. It sounds natural when it is fast and weak: /ˈsɔːtə/, /jə ˈnəʊ/. Listen for it, too – it is the part of small talk you can safely ignore.

L.p: Instructions are easier to follow when the speaker uses clear signal words and a clear voice. *Right* and *OK*, said with a fall, start a new stage. *OK?* with a rise checks that the listener is still with you. And the key words in each step are strongly stressed.

L.h: A starting and ordering the steps

L.say: Right. First of all, turn it off. Then open the lid – OK? Make sure you don't touch the blade.

L.p: Stress the action and the important object: *TURN the HANDLE, then PUSH*. Small words stay weak.

L.tip: Korean speakers: when you listen to instructions, the falling *Right.* or *OK.* is your signal that a new step is coming – it's a good moment to focus. When you give instructions, a rising *OK?* after each step invites people to ask questions.

L.p: When you repeat someone else's words – a saying, a title, a quote – you show it with your voice. People usually pause just before the quoted words, change their pitch a little, and often add a phrase like *as they say*.
*as they say*, *as the saying goes*, *in the words of…*, and in informal speech, *quote… unquote*. A saying is said as one chunk, with its own rhythm.

L.say: Well, better late than never, as they say.

L.p: Many English sayings have a strong rhythm, which makes them easy to remember. Say them as one unit.
When you report someone's exact words, many speakers change their voice to "act" the other person: *And he said, "I'm not paying!"*

L.say: And then she said, "Well, that's not my problem."

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has many four-character sayings and proverbs, and so does English. Learn the English ones as rhythm patterns: *PRACtice makes PERfect*, *EAsy COME, EAsy GO*.

L.p: In a neutral sentence the main stress falls on the last important word: *She can SWIM.* But you can move it to any word to add a special meaning – to contrast, to correct or to insist. This is emphatic stress, and it changes what the sentence tells the listener.
*SHE can swim* – she can, even if someone else can't. *She CAN swim* – it's true, although you said she couldn't. *She can SWIM* – the neutral version, or swimming in contrast to something else.

L.say: She can swim. She can swim! She can swim.

L.p: Make the emphasised word longer, louder and higher, with a big fall of the voice, and keep the rest of the sentence low and quiet. Even a small grammar word can be stressed this way: *I DID lock it!*

L.say: I didn't take your bike!

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean often shows emphasis with word order or particles such as -는 and -도. In English, the words usually stay in the same order and only the stress moves – so listen carefully for which word jumps out.

L.p: When you add a detail to make something clearer, the new detail takes the stress and the repeated words are weak: *I saw Anna – Anna from WORK.* *Meet me at the station – the BUS station.*
The words you repeat are already known, so they lose their stress. Only the extra information is strong.

L.say: I lost my bag – my black bag. We stayed in a hotel – a really cheap hotel.

L.p: The same thing happens when you answer *which one*: A: *Which jacket?* B: *The BLUE one.* *one* is weak because it repeats *jacket*.

L.say: Which jacket? The blue one. Which bus? The number nine.

L.tip: Korean speakers: if you stress every word in the detail – *my BLACK BAG* – the listener can't tell which part is new. Stress only the word that wasn't said before.

L.p: In every message there is one word that matters most – the one the listener really needs to hear. That word takes the main stress, and the others are said more quietly. This is especially important in polite complaints and corrections.
*Excuse me – I ordered the FISH.* *Sorry, I think that's MY coat.* *I asked for a SMALL one.* The stress does the work, so the words can stay polite.

L.say: Excuse me, I think that's my coat. Sorry, I asked for a small one.

L.h: The important word is not always last

L.p: *I wanted to go on FRIDAY* is neutral. *I WANTED to go on Friday* (but I couldn't) and *I wanted to GO on Friday* (not stay) say something different.

L.say: I wanted to go on Friday, but the trains were full.

L.tip: Korean speakers: in Korean, a complaint is often softened with endings and politeness levels. In English, the polite words (*Excuse me*, *Sorry*, *I think*) do the softening, and the stress quietly points to the problem. Keep your voice calm and let the important word stand out.

L.p: When you offer a choice, the stress and tune show the alternatives. In a choice question the voice rises on the first option and falls on the last: *Would you like TEA ↗ or COFfee ↘?* If it rises at the end instead, it is a yes/no question: *Would you like tea or coffee ↗?* means "Would you like something to drink?"

L.say: Would you like rice or pasta? Rice, please.

L.p: When the options share most of their words, stress the part that is different: *Is it THIS Friday or NEXT Friday?* *Do you want the RED one or the BLUE one?*

L.say: Is it this Friday or next Friday? Do you want the red one or the blue one?

L.tip: Korean speakers: a rising tune on both options can confuse an English listener – they may answer *Yes, please!* Make the last option fall clearly when you want the listener to choose.

L.p: When you correct someone, the correction takes a strong stress – even if it is only part of a word. A: *Is it on the third floor?* B: *No, the FOURTH.* A: *Did you say "possible"?* B: *No, IMpossible.*
Stress the word that is different, and let the rest be quiet: *Not my brother – my COUSIN.*

L.p: When two words differ only in their beginning, stress the beginning, even if it is not normally stressed: *I said EXport, not IMport.* *Not APpear – DISappear.*

L.say: I didn't say import, I said export. Not appear – disappear!

L.tip: Korean speakers: it can feel rude to correct someone with strong stress, but in English it is clear and normal – the stress quickly shows the mistake without a long explanation. Add *sorry* or *actually* if you want to sound softer: *Actually, it's the FOURTH floor.*

L.p: On the main stressed word of each chunk, the voice moves – and the direction it moves is called the tone. English uses three main tones, and they change the meaning of what you say, even of one single word.

A fall ↘ sounds definite and finished: *↘Yes.* (I'm sure.) A rise ↗ sounds questioning, unfinished or inviting: *↗Yes?* (What do you want? Go on.) A fall-rise ↘↗ sounds doubtful or incomplete, as if there is a "but" coming: *↘↗Yes…* (but…).

L.say: Yes. Yes? Yes…

L.p: The tone starts on the main stressed syllable and continues to the end of the chunk: *I'm from ↘KOrea*, *Is it ↗YOURS?*
*↘Fine.* – I agree. *↗Fine?* – Are you sure it's fine? *↘↗Fine…* – OK, but I'm not happy about it.

L.say: Fine. Fine? Fine…

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean uses tones at the ends of sentences too (-요 can rise or fall), so the idea is familiar. The difference is that in English the movement starts on the main stressed word, not on the last syllable.

L.p: A rising tone often means "I'm checking" or "Is that right?" You can turn almost any word or statement into a checking question just by using a rise, with no change to the grammar: *Today ↗?* *You're leaving ↗?*
A: *The train leaves at ten.* B: *↗Ten?* A: *Yes, ↘ten.* The rise checks; the fall confirms.

L.say: The train leaves at ten. Ten? Yes, ten.

L.p: *You're from Seoul ↗?* sounds like a question, though it looks like a statement. You often use this when you think you know the answer but want to check.

L.say: You're from Seoul? So you're a student?

L.p: Friends often add a rising *right ↗?* to the last word they say, to check a fact: *We're meeting at six, ↗right?*

L.tip: Korean speakers: in English, you can check information politely with just a rise – there is no need for a full question every time. And when someone checks with you, answer with a clear fall to show you are sure.

L.p: Questions that start with *what*, *where*, *when*, *who*, *why* or *how* usually have a falling tone: *Where do you ↘work?* The fall sounds natural and confident; the question word already shows it is a question.

L.p: In one sentence, some information is already known (old) and some is new. The new information usually has a fall ↘. The old or background information often has a fall-rise ↘↗, which says "this is what we're talking about – now here's the news".
*On ↘↗MONday, | we're open ↘LATE.* Monday is the topic; *late* is the news. *My ↘↗SISter | lives in ↘LONdon.*

L.say: On Monday, we're open late. My sister lives in London.

L.p: If the new information comes first, it takes the fall, and the rest of the sentence is said low and level: *↘LONdon's where she lives.*
A fall-rise on its own can show that you only partly agree: A: *Was the hotel nice?* B: *The ↘↗ROOM was nice…* (but the rest wasn't).

L.say: Was the hotel nice? The room was nice…

L.tip: Korean speakers: the fall-rise is a very English tune, and it can be hard to hear. Listen for it at the start of sentences (the topic) and in answers that seem to stop early – it often means there is a "but" that the speaker doesn't say.

L.p: A fall at the end of a chunk says "I've finished". A rise or a fall-rise says "there's more to come" – so the listener waits. This is how speakers keep a turn, read lists and build long sentences.
*When I got ↘↗HOME, | I had a ↘SHOWer.* The first chunk rises, so the listener waits; the fall on *shower* finishes the idea.

L.say: When I got home, I had a shower.

L.p: In a list the voice rises on each item and falls on the last: *We need ↗MILK, ↗BREAD and ↘EGGS.* If the list is open – there could be more – the last item rises too: *We need ↗milk, ↗bread, ↗eggs…*

L.say: We need milk, bread and eggs.

L.p: Listeners also use tones. *Oh ↗really?* with a rise invites the speaker to go on; *↘Really.* with a low fall can mean you are not very interested.

L.tip: Korean speakers: if each chunk of your sentence falls, listeners may think you have finished and start talking. Keep the voice up at the end of a chunk when you have more to say – it holds your turn without any extra words.

L.p: A question tag – *isn't it?*, *don't you?*, *have they?* – can rise or fall, and the tone changes its meaning. A fall means "I'm sure – please agree"; a rise means "I'm not sure – please tell me".
*It's a lovely day, ↘ISn't it?* *You know Sam, ↘DON'T you?* The speaker expects *yes*.

L.say: It's a lovely day, isn't it?

L.p: *The shop's open on Sundays, ↗ISn't it?* The speaker doesn't know and wants to check.

L.say: The shop's open on Sundays, isn't it?

L.p: Agreeing replies usually fall and sound warm.
Polite disagreement often starts with a fall-rise, which softens it: *↘↗WELL…*, *I'm not ↘↗SURE…*

L.p: To sound enthusiastic, surprised or impressed, English speakers start the main stressed word very high and let the voice fall a long way. A low start with a small fall sounds bored – even if the words are positive.
*That's ↘FANtastic!* *How ↘LOVEly!* The higher the start, the stronger the feeling.

L.say: That's fantastic! How lovely!

L.p: A very high rise shows disbelief or great surprise: *You ↗DIDN'T!* *↗REALly?!*

L.say: Really? You didn't!

L.tip: Korean speakers: English speakers often use a wider pitch range than Korean speakers do, and a narrow range can sound flat or unfriendly to them. Don't be shy about going high – it sounds warm and natural in English, not exaggerated.
